sections.title: What does "1 in 6" mean?

blocks.html:
A die has a "1 in 6 chance" of showing a 4. But roll it six times and you almost never get exactly one 4. So what is that 1 in 6 a promise about?

It's a promise about the long run. Roll a thousand times and close to a sixth of the rolls are 4s. Roll a million times and it's closer still. Nobody can predict one roll, but a pile of rolls is very predictable.

Before any formulas, roll some dice. Start with two dice and look at the shape the sums make.

blocks.name: ps-dice
blocks.title: Rolling in bulk
blocks.goal: Roll two dice until your estimate of P(sum = 7) is within 0.01 of the truth (needs at least 500 rolls). Then switch the ghost to the naive guess and see why "all sums equally likely" is wrong.
blocks.intro: Set Rolls per press to 1,000 and press Roll a few times. Click a column to see which pairs of dice make that sum.

blocks.q: You roll two dice and add them. Which sum comes up most often in the long run?

opts.t: 12, because it's the biggest
They're all equally likely: there are 11 sums and each has a 1 in 11 chance
7, because more pairs of dice add up to 7 than to any other sum
2 and 12, because they're at the ends

blocks.why: There are 6 × 6 = 36 equally likely pairs (die 1, die 2). Six of them make 7: 1+6, 2+5, 3+4, 4+3, 5+2, 6+1. Only one makes 2 (1+1). That's why the columns form a triangle.

sections.title: Outcomes, sample spaces and events

blocks.html:
Three words do all the work in probability:

  • An outcome is one thing that can happen: the die shows 4.
  • The sample space is the list of every outcome: {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}.
  • An event is a group of outcomes you care about: "an even number" is {2, 4, 6}.

When every outcome is equally likely, the probability of an event is just counting: how many outcomes are in the event, divided by how many there are in total. Even number: 3 out of 6, so 1/2.

For two dice, the sample space is every pair. itertools.product builds it for you.

blocks.code:
space = list(itertools.product(range(1, 7), repeat=2))
print(len(space))
print(space[:3])
sevens = [pair for pair in space if sum(pair) == 7]
print(len(sevens))
print(len(sevens) / len(space))

blocks.html: Why pairs, and not just the 11 sums? Because the pairs are equally likely and the sums are not. The red ghost in the simulation is what you get if you forget this.

sections.title: Probability is a long-run frequency

blocks.html:
Counting works when the outcomes are equally likely and few. When they aren't, we simulate: do the experiment many times on the computer and count.

np.random.default_rng(seed) makes a random number generator. Giving it a seed means you get the same "random" numbers every run, so you can check results. rng.integers(1, 7, size=n) rolls n dice (the 7 is excluded, like range).

blocks.code:
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
rolls = rng.integers(1, 7, size=10)
print(rolls)
for n in [10, 1000, 100000]:
    rolls = rng.integers(1, 7, size=n)
    print(n, round(float(np.mean(rolls == 4)), 2))

blocks.html: Notice rolls == 4 makes an array of True/False, and the mean of that is the fraction of rolls that were 4. That one line is the workhorse of this whole track.

blocks.prompt: Estimate P(sum of two dice = 7) by simulation. Fill the blanks: roll two arrays of dice, add them, and return the fraction of sums equal to target.

assert abs(est - 6 / 36) < 0.005, f"With 200,000 rolls the estimate of P(7) should be very close to 0.1667, got {est:.4f}"
assert abs(estimate_sum(2, 200_000) - 1 / 36) < 0.003, "Only (1,1) makes 2, so P(2) is about 1/36 = 0.028"

sections.title: Counting without listing

blocks.html:
Listing every outcome stops working fast: a 5-card poker hand has millions. So we count with three rules.

  1. Multiplication rule. If you make one choice with a options and then another with b options, there are a × b combinations. Two dice: 6 × 6 = 36. A 4-digit PIN: 10 × 10 × 10 × 10.
  2. Permutations (order matters, no repeats). Gold, silver and bronze among 8 runners: 8 × 7 × 6 = 336. That's math.perm(8, 3).
  3. Combinations (order doesn't matter). Picking 3 people for a team from 8: each team was counted 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 times in the permutations (once per ordering), so 336 / 6 = 56. That's math.comb(8, 3).

blocks.code:
print(10 ** 4)
print(math.perm(8, 3))
print(math.comb(8, 3))
print(math.perm(8, 3) // math.factorial(3))
print(math.comb(52, 5))

blocks.html: The question to ask every time: does the order matter? Medals: yes (gold ≠ silver). A team or a poker hand: no.

sections.title: The birthday problem

blocks.html:
How many people do you need in a room before there's a better than even chance that two share a birthday? Most people guess around 180. The real answer is 23.

Counting trick: it's easier to find the chance that nobody shares. The first person can have any of 365 days, the second must avoid that one (364 left), the third must avoid two (363 left), and so on. Then the chance someone does share is 1 minus that. (Using "1 minus the opposite" is called the complement; it gets its own step next chapter.)

blocks.code:
p_none = 1.0
for i in range(23):
    p_none *= (365 - i) / 365
print(round(p_none, 3))
print(round(1 - p_none, 3))

blocks.html:
Why so few? Because with 23 people there are math.comb(23, 2) = 253 pairs, and any pair can match. You were probably picturing someone matching you, which is only 22 pairs.

Now check it the simulation way: give 23 people random birthdays, many times, and count the rooms with a repeat.

blocks.solution:
def simulate_matches(trials, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    numbers = np.arange(1, 50)
    counts = [0] * 7
    for _ in range(trials):
        win = rng.choice(numbers, size=6, replace=False)
        ticket = rng.choice(numbers, size=6, replace=False)
        k = len(set(win) & set(ticket))
        counts[k] += 1
    return [c / trials for c in counts]

sections.title: Does knowing one thing change the odds of another?

blocks.html:
A shop has 400 customers. Some bought bread, some bought butter. If I tell you a customer bought butter, is it now more likely they bought bread? And if I tell you they shopped at the weekend, does that tell you anything about the butter?

The simulation shows each customer as one block. Colour shows two yes/no facts about them: A and B. Pressing Given B lifts the B customers out of the crowd. Asking "what's the chance of A, given B?" just means: among the lifted people, what fraction are A?

blocks.q: In the "Bread & butter" scenario, 120 customers buy butter and 96 of those also buy bread. What is P(bread | butter)?
blocks.why: "Given butter" means we only look at the 120 butter buyers. 96 of them bought bread, so 96/120 = 0.8. Dividing by 400 would answer a different question: P(bread and butter).

sections.title: The complement and the addition rule

blocks.html:
Two rules come straight from counting.

Complement. Every outcome is either in event A or not. So P(not A) = 1 − P(A). This is often the easy way in: "at least one six in four rolls" is hard to count directly, but "no sixes" is just (5/6)⁴.

Addition rule. P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). Why subtract? If you add the A people and the B people, everyone who is both got counted twice. Take them away once.
The naive answer for "even or big" is 3 + 3 = 6 outcomes, which would be certain. But 1 and 3 are neither! The overlap {4, 6} was counted twice.

blocks.title: p_or
blocks.prompt: Fill in the addition rule, then use the complement for p_at_least_one_six(rolls): the chance of at least one six in rolls rolls of a fair die.

assert abs(p_at_least_one_six(4) - 0.5177) < 1e-4, f"Four rolls: about 0.518, got {p_at_least_one_six(4)}"

sections.title: Conditional probability: count inside the smaller world

blocks.html:
The notation P(A | B) reads "probability of A given B". The recipe is what the simulation does:

  1. Throw away everyone who isn't B (they fade out).
  2. Among who's left, count the A's.

As a formula: P(A | B) = (number who are A and B) / (number who are B). Divide the top and bottom by the total and you get the textbook version, P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B). It's the same thing.

Careful: P(A | B) and P(B | A) are different. The fraction of butter buyers who buy bread is 96/120 = 0.8. The fraction of bread buyers who buy butter is 96/180 = 0.53. Different bottom number, different world.

sections.title: Independence and the multiplication rule

blocks.html:
Two events are independent when learning one doesn't change the chance of the other: P(A | B) = P(A). In the weekend scenario, the fraction of butter buyers among weekend shoppers is about the same as overall: the day tells you nothing about butter.

Rearranging the conditional formula gives the multiplication rule, which always works:

P(A and B) = P(B) × P(A | B)

When A and B are independent, P(A | B) is just P(A), so it shrinks to P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). That shortcut is why we could multiply dice in chapter 1. Using it when events are not independent is one of the most common mistakes in real analysis: rain and umbrellas, or two components failing in the same storm.

blocks.title: An independence test from counts
blocks.tests:
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
x = rng.random(100000) < 0.4
y = rng.random(100000) < 0.5
assert looks_independent(x, y), "Two separate random draws are independent"
assert not looks_independent(x, x), "An event is never independent of itself (unless P is 0 or 1)"

blocks.q: P(rain) = 0.3 and P(I carry an umbrella) = 0.4. Someone computes P(rain and umbrella) = 0.3 × 0.4 = 0.12. What's wrong?

opts.t: Nothing, that's the multiplication rule
They should have added: 0.3 + 0.4 = 0.7
They assumed independence, but I'm much more likely to carry an umbrella when it rains, so the real answer is bigger
Probabilities can't be multiplied

blocks.why: The general rule is P(rain and umbrella) = P(rain) × P(umbrella | rain). If P(umbrella | rain) is 0.9, the answer is 0.27, more than twice 0.12. Multiplying the plain probabilities is only allowed when the events are independent.

sections.title: Tree diagrams: one stage at a time

blocks.html:
A bag has 3 red and 2 blue marbles. Draw two without putting the first back. What's P(both red)?

Draw it as a tree. The first branch: red with 3/5. Now the bag has changed (2 red, 2 blue), so the second branch, given the first was red, is 2/4. Multiply along a path: 3/5 × 2/4 = 6/20 = 0.3. That's the multiplication rule with a picture.

To get P(second is red) you add up every path that ends in red: (red, red) + (blue, red) = 3/5 × 2/4 + 2/5 × 3/4 = 0.6. Same as the first draw, which surprises most people.

sections.title: Monty Hall: let the computer settle the argument

blocks.html:
A game show has three doors: a car behind one, goats behind two. You pick a door. The host, who knows where the car is, opens one of the other doors to show a goat, then offers you a swap. Should you switch?

Almost everyone says "two doors left, so it's 50/50". Professional mathematicians wrote angry letters saying so in 1990. They were wrong: switching wins 2/3 of the time. Your first pick is right 1/3 of the time. The other 2/3, the car is behind one of the two doors you didn't pick, and the host is forced to open the other one, so switching takes you straight to the car.

When intuition fights, simulate. Play by hand first, then a few hundred games each way.

def monty_hall(switch, games, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    wins = 0
    for _ in range(games):
        car = rng.integers(0, 3)
        pick = rng.integers(0, 3)
        opened = [d for d in range(3) if d != pick and d != car][0]
        if switch:
            pick = [d for d in range(3) if d != pick and d != opened][0]
        wins += pick == car
    return wins / games

sections.title: Real-world project: "customers who bought this also bought…"

blocks.html: Every online shop shows "people who buy X also buy Y". Under the hood that's conditional probability on shopping baskets, a technique called association rules.

blocks.title: Basket analysis for a corner shop
blocks.client: A corner shop that wants to know what to put next to what
blocks.brief: The shop gives you its till receipts: each basket is a set of items. For a rule "X → Y" compute three numbers: support P(X and Y) (how common the pair is), confidence P(Y | X) (of baskets with X, how many have Y), and lift P(Y | X) / P(Y). Lift is the independence test in disguise: lift ≈ 1 means X tells you nothing about Y; lift 2 means X doubles the chance of Y. Recommend the rules with the highest lift that aren't too rare.
blocks.why: This is the classic "market basket analysis" used by supermarkets for shelf layout, by Amazon-style recommenders, by streaming apps ("viewers of this also watched"), and in fraud detection (which events happen together more than chance). Confidence alone misleads: milk is in most baskets, so "anything → milk" has high confidence but lift near 1.

sections.title: You tested positive. Are you sick?

blocks.html:
A disease affects 1 in 100 people. A test catches 90% of sick people, and wrongly flags 9% of healthy people. You test positive. What's the chance you have the disease?

Most people (and, in studies, most doctors) say about 90%. The real answer is about 9%. Not a typo.

Instead of a formula, picture 1,000 people. The simulation shows them as blocks. Sick people are red, everyone takes the test, and positives rise into the air. The question is just: of the people in the air, how many are red?

blocks.name: ps-bayes
blocks.title: 1,000 people take a test
blocks.goal: Find settings with sensitivity and specificity both at least 90%, where a positive test still means under 20% chance of being sick.
blocks.intro: Start at 10% prevalence. Then lower the prevalence and watch the amber false positives take over the raised group. Click a block to see its group.

blocks.q: In a town of 1,000, 10 people are sick. The test catches 9 of them, and also flags 89 of the 990 healthy people. Of everyone who tests positive, what fraction is sick?

opts.t: 89 / 990 ≈ 9%, which is a coincidence

blocks.why: Everyone who tests positive is 9 + 89 = 98 people, and only 9 of them are sick. The 90% is the share of sick people who test positive, a different question with a different bottom number.

sections.title: Natural frequencies: just count people

blocks.html:
The trick that makes Bayes easy is to stop thinking in percentages and count people instead. Four numbers describe the whole situation:

  • Prevalence (also called the prior or base rate): what fraction is sick before any test. 1%.
  • Sensitivity: of the sick, what fraction test positive. 90%.
  • Specificity: of the healthy, what fraction test negative. 91%, so 9% of the healthy get a false positive.
  • The posterior: what we actually want, P(sick | positive).

Now push 1,000 people through it.

blocks.code:
people = 1000
sick = people * 0.01
healthy = people - sick
true_pos = sick * 0.90
false_pos = healthy * (1 - 0.91)
print(round(sick), round(healthy))
print(round(true_pos), round(false_pos))
print(round(true_pos / (true_pos + false_pos), 3))

blocks.html: The false positives win because 9% of 990 is much bigger than 90% of 10. The test is fine; the disease is just rare.

assert abs(fp - 89.1) < 1e-9, f"990 healthy, 9% wrongly flagged: 89.1 false positives, got {fp}"
tp, fp = positives_table(100, 0.5, 1.0, 1.0)
assert tp == 50 and fp == 0, "A perfect test has no false positives"

    sick = n * prevalence

blocks.solution:
def positives_table(n, prevalence, sensitivity, specificity):
    sick = n * prevalence
    healthy = n - sick
    true_pos = sick * sensitivity
    false_pos = healthy * (1 - specificity)
    return true_pos, false_pos

sections.title: Bayes' rule is the same counting

blocks.html:
Divide every count by the number of people and you get the formula known as Bayes' rule:

P(sick | +) = P(+ | sick) × P(sick) / P(+)

where P(+), the chance of testing positive at all, is the sum of both raised groups: P(+ | sick) × P(sick) + P(+ | healthy) × P(healthy). Top: the true positives. Bottom: all positives. It's exactly true_pos / (true_pos + false_pos), with fractions instead of people.

The naive answer swaps the two conditionals: it reports P(+ | sick) (the sensitivity) when you asked for P(sick | +). Swapping them has a name, the prosecutor's fallacy, because it has put innocent people in prison ("only 1 in a million innocent people would match this evidence" is not "1 in a million chance he's innocent").

sections.title: Why rare things fool good tests

blocks.html: Keep the test fixed and change only the prevalence. Same test, wildly different meaning.

A 95%/95% test is nearly useless for screening a 1-in-1,000 disease on its own: 98% of positives are false alarms. That's why screening programmes use a cheap first test and then a second, different test on the positives. It's also why airport scanners, fraud alerts and smoke alarms "cry wolf" so often: the thing they look for is rare.

sections.title: Updating twice

blocks.html:
You test positive, so you take a second, independent test, and it's positive too. What now?

Bayes chains: after the first test, your posterior (9%) becomes the prior for the second test. Feed it back in. Each positive multiplies the odds by the same factor, so belief climbs fast. Press Test the positives again in the simulation to see the false positives mostly drop out.

sections.title: From tests to words: spam

blocks.html: A spam filter is a medical test where the "disease" is spam and the "symptoms" are words. Say 40% of email is spam, the word "free" appears in 30% of spam and 2% of normal mail. You see "free". Same machine:

blocks.code:
p_spam = 0.4
p_free_given_spam = 0.30
p_free_given_ham = 0.02
top = p_spam * p_free_given_spam

print(round(top, 3), round(bottom, 3))

blocks.html: With many words, the filter updates once per word, as if each word were another independent test. Words aren't really independent ("free" and "prize" travel together), which is why it's called naive Bayes. It works surprisingly well anyway.

blocks.q: Why do spam filters add up logarithms of probabilities instead of multiplying the probabilities?

opts.t: Logarithms make the answer more accurate in principle
Multiplying hundreds of small numbers like 0.001 rounds to 0.0 in floating point; adding logs keeps the information
Python can't multiply more than 100 numbers
Logarithms remove the "naive" assumption

blocks.why: log(a × b) = log a + log b, so the comparison is the same, but 0.001²⁰⁰ is 10⁻⁶⁰⁰, far below the smallest float (about 10⁻³⁰⁸). In logs it's just −1381.6, perfectly fine.

The same "prior × evidence" logic runs medical decision tools, fraud scores and A/B testing dashboards.

sections.title: A board full of coin flips

blocks.html: Drop a ball onto a board of pegs. At every peg it goes left or right at random. Where does it land? You can't say for one ball. But drop a few hundred and a very definite shape appears, and you can predict that shape before dropping a single ball.

blocks.name: ps-galton
blocks.title: The Galton board
blocks.goal: Tilt the board (set p at least 0.1 away from 0.5), drop 500 balls, and get your pile to match the formula's ghosts within 6%.
blocks.intro: Each ball goes right at each peg with probability p. The bin it lands in is the number of rights. Amber ghosts are what the binomial formula predicts. Click anything to ask why.

blocks.q: With p = 0.5 and 10 rows, why do so many balls land in the middle bin (5 rights) and so few at the edges (0 or 10 rights)?

opts.t: The pegs in the middle are bigger
Balls bounce toward the centre
Only one route gives 0 rights (left every time), but 252 different routes give exactly 5 rights
It's luck; with more balls it would even out

blocks.why: Every single route is equally likely when p = 0.5. The middle bin wins because far more routes end there. Counting those routes is what the binomial formula does.

sections.title: A random variable is just a number from an outcome

blocks.html: Flip 3 coins. The outcome is something like HTH. A random variable is any number you compute from the outcome: the number of heads (2), whether the first is heads (1), the longest run (1). Calling it X and asking "what values can X take, and how often?" is the whole game.

blocks.code:
from itertools import product
outcomes = list(product("HT", repeat=3))
heads = [o.count("H") for o in outcomes]
print(len(outcomes))
print(sorted(heads))
print({k: heads.count(k) for k in range(4)})

blocks.html: The table of "value → probability" is the variable's distribution. For a variable with separate values, it's called the PMF (probability mass function). Its running total, P(X ≤ x), is the CDF (cumulative distribution function). The CDF is handy because any range is a subtraction: P(a < X ≤ b) = CDF(b) − CDF(a).

sections.title: The binomial: counting the routes

blocks.html:
The Galton board is n independent yes/no trials with the same chance p of "yes" each time (a Bernoulli trial). The number of yeses follows the binomial distribution:

P(X = k) = C(n, k) · pᵏ · (1 − p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ

Read it as a sentence: the number of routes with k yeses × the chance of any one such route. C(n, k) ("n choose k", math.comb(n, k)) counts the routes; pᵏ(1−p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ is the chance of each one, because the trials are independent and their probabilities multiply.

It fits whenever all four hold: a fixed number of trials, two outcomes each, the same p, and independence. Free-throw makes, defective items in a batch, and patients who respond to a drug are all binomial.

def at_least(k, n, p):
    return sum(math.comb(n, j) * p ** j * (1 - p) ** (n - j) for j in range(k, n + 1))

sections.title: Waiting for something: geometric and Poisson

blocks.html:
Two more counting distributions come up constantly:

  • Geometric: how many tries until the first success? (Rolls until a six, calls until a sale.) P(first success on try k) = (1 − p)ᵏ⁻¹ · p. Its average is 1/p.
  • Poisson: how many events in a fixed window, when they happen independently at an average rate λ? (Calls per minute, typos per page, goals per match.) P(X = k) = λᵏ e^(−λ) / k!. Its average and its variance are both λ.

blocks.html:
Heights, times and temperatures can take any value in a range. Then the chance of hitting one exact value, like exactly 1.500000… m, is zero: there are infinitely many neighbours sharing the probability. Instead, a PDF (probability density function) is a curve, and the probability of a range is the area under it. The CDF still works the same way.

The three you'll meet most:

DistributionShapeTypical use
uniform(a, b)flata random point in a range
exponential(rate λ)high at 0, decayingwaiting time between Poisson events

blocks.q: Bus waits are exponential with an average of 10 minutes. You've already waited 10 minutes. How long do you expect to wait now?

5 minutes
10 more minutes: the exponential has no memory
20 minutes

blocks.why: The exponential is memoryless: P(wait > s + t | waited s) = P(wait > t). If buses truly arrive like a Poisson process, the time you've already waited tells you nothing. (Real buses on a timetable aren't like this, which is why the model choice matters.)

blocks.solution:
def binomial_table(n, p):
    return [math.comb(n, k) * p ** k * (1 - p) ** (n - k) for k in range(n + 1)]

blocks.q: Explain the binomial formula C(n, k) pᵏ (1−p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ using the Galton board, and say when you'd use Poisson instead.
blocks.a: Each peg is a yes/no trial with chance p of "right". A ball's bin is its number of rights k. Any single route with k rights and n−k lefts has probability pᵏ(1−p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ because independent chances multiply, and there are C(n, k) such routes, so you multiply the two. Use Poisson when there's no fixed number of trials, just events happening independently at a steady average rate λ in a window of time or space (calls per minute, typos per page).

sections.title: What does "95% confident" actually mean?

blocks.html:
A food-delivery startup times 10 deliveries. The average is 33.1 minutes. Is the real average (over all deliveries, forever) 33.1? Almost certainly not exactly: a different 10 deliveries would give a different average. You learned in chapter 7 that sample averages wobble.

So instead of one number, we report a range: "between 27.9 and 38.3 minutes". The range is a net we throw at an invisible target. Here is the key idea, and it surprises most people:

The 95% is a property of the net-throwing method, not of any one net. If you threw 100 nets this way, about 95 would catch the truth.

Any single net either caught it or didn't. You just don't know which. Throw 100 nets and see.

blocks.name: ps-ci
blocks.title: 100 samples, 100 intervals, one truth
blocks.goal: Draw intervals at three different settings, changing both the confidence level and n. Watch how many bars go red and how wide they get.
blocks.intro: Each bar is one interval from one sample. Click a bar to see its sample. Then switch to z = 1.96 with s (naive) at n = 5 and count the red bars.

blocks.q: You build a 95% interval for average delivery time and get 28 to 35 minutes. Which statement is correct?

opts.t: There is a 95% chance the true average is between 28 and 35
95% of deliveries take between 28 and 35 minutes
The method that produced 28 to 35 catches the true average in about 95% of samples
If you repeat the study, 95% of new averages will land between 28 and 35

blocks.why: The true average is a fixed number; it's either in [28, 35] or not. The 95% describes how often the procedure works. (The second option mixes up the average with single deliveries, which vary much more.)

sections.title: How much does an average wobble?

blocks.html: Before building any interval we need one number: how far a sample average typically lands from the truth. Commit to a guess first.

blocks.code:
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
samples = rng.normal(32, 8, size=(2000, 25))   # 2000 rows, 25 deliveries each
means = samples.mean(axis=1)
print("sd of single deliveries:", round(samples.std(), 1))
print("sd of the averages:     ", round(means.std(), 1))
blocks.title: Deliveries have sd 8 min. Take 2000 samples of 25 deliveries each. What is the sd of the 2000 averages?

blocks.html:
The averages wobble 5 times less than single deliveries, and 5 = √25. That number has a name: the standard error (SE), the standard deviation of a statistic across samples:

SE of the mean = σ / √n

We never know σ, so we plug in the sample's own standard deviation s (with ddof=1, dividing by n − 1, because a sample's spread around its own average is a little too small).

Why √n and not n? Because errors partly cancel. Ten deliveries don't make the average 10 times more precise, only √10 ≈ 3.2 times. To halve the error you need four times the data. Check it:

blocks.code:
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
for n in [25, 100, 400]:
    means = rng.normal(32, 8, size=(2000, n)).mean(axis=1)
    print(f"n = {n:4d}   sd of averages = {means.std():.2f}   formula 8/sqrt(n) = {8/np.sqrt(n):.2f}")
blocks.title: Quadruple n, halve the wobble
standard_error

The second blank is np.sqrt(len(sample)).

sections.title: Building the net: average ± 2 standard errors

blocks.html:
From chapter 6: a normal value lands within 1.96 standard deviations of its centre 95% of the time. The sample average is (nearly) normal around the truth, with sd = SE. So the truth is within 1.96 SE of the average 95% of the time. Flip that around and you get the net:

average ± 1.96 × SE

If the "95% of the time" claim is real, we can check it by simulation: make many samples, build a net from each, count catches. Guess first.

blocks.code:
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
n, caught = 20, 0
for _ in range(10000):
    x = rng.normal(32, 8, n)
    m, se = x.mean(), 8 / np.sqrt(n)
    if m - 1.96 * se <= 32 <= m + 1.96 * se:
        caught += 1
print(round(caught / 10000, 2))
blocks.title: We know σ = 8 here. Out of 10000 nets built as mean ± 1.96·8/√n, about what fraction catch 32?

blocks.html: That is the honest meaning of "95%": it's a coverage rate you can measure. Other levels just change the multiplier: 1.645 for 90%, 2.576 for 99%. A higher level means a wider net, which is the price of missing less.

blocks.title: A z-interval function
lines: return (m - z * se, m + z * se)
distractors: return (m - z * sample.std(), m + z * sample.std())

blocks.q: You switch from a 95% net (multiplier 1.96) to a 99% net (multiplier 2.576) on the same data. What happens?

opts.t: The interval gets narrower, because you're more confident
The interval gets about 31% wider, and misses about 1 in 100 instead of 1 in 20
Nothing changes; confidence only affects the wording
The average moves closer to the truth

blocks.why: More confidence costs width: 2.576 / 1.96 ≈ 1.31. The only way to get both narrow and confident is more data.

sections.title: Small samples need t

blocks.html: The z-interval quietly assumes we know σ. We don't; we use s, and with a small sample s itself wobbles. Sometimes it comes out too small, and the net shrinks just when it should be wide. How bad is that?

blocks.code:
rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
n, caught = 5, 0
for _ in range(10000):
    x = rng.normal(32, 8, n)
    m, se = x.mean(), x.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(n)
    if m - 1.96 * se <= 32 <= m + 1.96 * se:
        caught += 1
print(round(caught / 10000, 2))
blocks.title: Same check, but n = 5 and we plug in s instead of the true σ. Fraction caught with 1.96?

blocks.html: A "95%" net that catches only about 88% of the time is lying. In 1908 William Gosset, a brewer at Guinness testing small batches of barley, worked out the fix: use a slightly bigger multiplier that depends on the sample size. It comes from the t distribution with n − 1 "degrees of freedom". For n = 5 the 95% multiplier is 2.78 instead of 1.96; by n = 30 it's 2.05, nearly the normal value.

blocks.code:
from scipy import stats
for n in [3, 5, 10, 30, 100]:
    print(f"n = {n:3d}   t multiplier = {stats.t.ppf(0.975, n - 1):.3f}")
print("normal       =", round(stats.norm.ppf(0.975), 3))
blocks.title: The t multiplier shrinks toward 1.96 as n grows

blocks.html: Why 0.975 and not 0.95? A 95% interval leaves 5% outside, split into 2.5% on each side. So the upper cut is at the 97.5% point.

blocks.title: t_interval

sections.title: The bootstrap: when there is no formula

blocks.html:
σ/√n is the SE of a mean. What about the median delivery time, or the 90th percentile (the "slow" deliveries customers remember)? There's no tidy formula. The bootstrap, invented by Bradley Efron in 1979, says: your sample is your best picture of the population, so resample from it (with replacement, same size), recompute the statistic, and repeat a few thousand times. The spread of those recomputed values is the SE.

First, what does one resample look like?

blocks.code:
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
data = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
res = rng.choice(data, size=len(data), replace=True)
print(sorted(res.tolist()))
print("distinct:", len(set(res)))
blocks.title: Resample [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] with replacement. How many distinct values will it contain?

blocks.html: Some values repeat and some vanish; on average a resample contains only about 63% of the distinct originals. That missing-and-doubling is exactly the variation a fresh sample would have. Why with replacement? Without it, every resample would be the original data shuffled, with the same median every time and zero spread: useless.

blocks.code:
rng = np.random.default_rng(6)
times = np.array([22, 25, 26, 28, 29, 30, 31, 31, 33, 35, 38, 41, 44, 52, 67])
meds = np.array([np.median(rng.choice(times, len(times))) for _ in range(5000)])
lo, hi = np.percentile(meds, [2.5, 97.5])
print("sample median:", np.median(times))
print("bootstrap SE: ", round(meds.std(), 2))
print("95% bootstrap interval:", lo, "to", hi)
blocks.title: Bootstrap the median of 15 deliveries

blocks.html: Taking the middle 95% of the bootstrap values is called the percentile interval. Back in the simulation, choose bootstrap and press Show resamples of #1 to see the skyline of resample averages.

blocks.title: bootstrap_ci
blocks.prompt: Write bootstrap_ci(data, stat, B=2000, conf=0.95, seed=0). Make a generator with np.random.default_rng(seed), draw B resamples of the same size with replacement, apply stat (a function such as np.median) to each, and return the (lower, upper) percentile interval.
blocks.tests:
times = np.array([22, 25, 26, 28, 29, 30, 31, 31, 33, 35, 38, 41, 44, 52, 67])
lo, hi = bootstrap_ci(times, np.median)
assert lo < 31 < hi, f"the interval should contain the sample median 31; got ({lo}, {hi})"
assert 26 <= lo <= 31 and 31 <= hi <= 41, f"the median's interval should be roughly 28 to 38; got ({lo}, {hi})"
lo2, hi2 = bootstrap_ci(times, np.median, conf=0.5)
assert hi2 - lo2 < hi - lo, "a 50% interval must be narrower than a 95% one"
lo3, hi3 = bootstrap_ci(np.full(10, 7.0), np.mean)
assert lo3 == hi3 == 7.0, "data with no spread gives an interval of zero width"
hints: A list comprehension does it: [stat(rng.choice(data, size=len(data), replace=True)) for _ in range(B)].
For 95%, the cut points are the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles: np.percentile(vals, [2.5, 97.5]).
blocks.solution:
def bootstrap_ci(data, stat, B=2000, conf=0.95, seed=0):
    data = np.asarray(data)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    vals = np.array([stat(rng.choice(data, size=len(data), replace=True)) for _ in range(B)])
    tail = (1 - conf) / 2 * 100
    lo, hi = np.percentile(vals, [tail, 100 - tail])
    return (lo, hi)

sections.title: Planning: how many deliveries do we need?

blocks.html: The net's half-width is called the margin of error: about z × σ/√n. Turn that around and you can plan a study before collecting data: to get a margin of E you need n = (z·σ/E)².

blocks.code:
import math
for E in [2, 1, 0.5]:
    n = math.ceil((1.96 * 8 / E) ** 2)
    print(f"margin ±{E} min needs n = {n}")
blocks.title: With σ ≈ 8 min, how many deliveries for a 95% margin of ±1 min? And for ±0.5 min?

blocks.html: Halving the margin quadruples the cost. That's the √n law again, and it's why polls stop at about 1000 people: going from ±3% to ±1.5% would need 4000.

blocks.prompt: Write zone_report(zones). zones maps a zone name to a list of delivery times. Return a dict mapping each name to a tuple (mean, lo, hi, verdict) where (lo, hi) is a 95% t-interval and verdict is "late" if lo > 30, "on time" if hi < 30, otherwise "need more data".

assert r["B"][3] == "late", f"zone B (150 deliveries around 36 min) is clearly late; got {r['B']}"
assert abs(r["C"][0] - 34.0) < 1e-9, "zone C's mean is 34.0"
assert r["C"][3] == "need more data", f"zone C averages 34 but has only 7 noisy orders: its interval includes 30. Got {r['C']}"
assert r["C"][1] < 30 < r["C"][2], "zone C's interval should straddle 30"

The verdict is a three-way choice; a chained conditional expression or an if/elif/else works.
blocks.solution:
def zone_report(zones):
    report = {}
    for name, times in zones.items():
        x = np.asarray(times, dtype=float)
        n = len(x)
        m = x.mean()
        se = x.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(n)
        t = stats.t.ppf(0.975, n - 1)
        lo, hi = m - t * se, m + t * se
        verdict = "late" if lo > 30 else "on time" if hi < 30 else "need more data"
        report[name] = (m, lo, hi, verdict)
    return report

blocks.q: Explain to a friend what "a 95% confidence interval of 28 to 35 minutes" means, why the interval narrows as n grows, and why small samples use t instead of 1.96.
blocks.a: The procedure that made [28, 35] catches the true average in about 95 of 100 samples; this particular interval either caught it or didn't. Its width is about 2 × multiplier × s/√n, so it shrinks like 1/√n (4x the data halves it). With small n the sample sd s is itself unreliable and often too small, so 1.96 would under-cover (about 88% at n = 5); the t multiplier is larger for small n to make the promise true. When no formula exists (median, percentiles), resample the data with replacement (the bootstrap) and take the middle 95% of the recomputed statistic.

sections.title: Did the new design work?

blocks.html:
A website tried a new sign-up page for 8 days and kept the old one for 8 other days. Daily sign-ups:

  • old page: 31, 28, 35, 30, 27, 33, 29, 32
  • new page: 34, 30, 38, 33, 29, 36, 31, 37

The new page averages about 3 more sign-ups a day. But days vary anyway: some are just busier. So the real question is: if the page made no difference at all, how often would luck alone produce a gap this big?

Here's the trick that answers it with no formulas. If the page did nothing, the labels "old" and "new" are meaningless: any day could have worn either label. So shuffle the labels, recompute the gap, and repeat thousands of times. That pile of shuffled gaps is what luck looks like.

blocks.name: ps-permute
blocks.title: Shuffle the labels, see what luck looks like
blocks.goal: Shuffle at least 1,000 times to estimate the p-value, then try p-hacking: 20 tests on noise and run them.
blocks.intro: Each column is one day (its height is the sign-ups). Shuffle labels mixes which days count as old or new and drops the new gap into the histogram behind. The marker is the real gap.

blocks.q: After 1,000 shuffles, 21 of the shuffled gaps were at least as big as the real one. What does that tell you?

opts.t: There's a 2.1% chance the new page works
There's a 97.9% chance the new page works
If the page made no difference, luck alone would produce a gap this big about 2.1% of the time
The new page adds 2.1% more sign-ups

blocks.why: That's the definition of a p-value: the probability of data at least this extreme assuming the null hypothesis is true. It isn't the probability that the null (or the alternative) is true. That needs a prior: chapter 11.

sections.title: The null hypothesis and the test statistic

blocks.html:
Every test has the same skeleton:

  1. The null hypothesis (H₀): the boring explanation. "The page makes no difference."
  2. A test statistic: one number that measures the effect you care about. Here: mean(new) − mean(old).
  3. The null distribution: what that number looks like when H₀ is true. Shuffling builds it for us.
  4. The p-value: where the real number falls in that distribution.

Choosing the statistic is a modelling decision. The difference in means is natural, but you could compare medians if a few huge days worried you.

blocks.code:
old = np.array([31, 28, 35, 30, 27, 33, 29, 32])
new = np.array([34, 30, 38, 33, 29, 36, 31, 37])
print(new.mean(), old.mean())
print(new.mean() - old.mean())

blocks.solution:
def perm_test(a, b, n=10000, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    a, b = np.asarray(a, float), np.asarray(b, float)
    observed = b.mean() - a.mean()
    pooled = np.concatenate([a, b])
    count = 0
    for _ in range(n):
        m = rng.permutation(pooled)
        if m[len(a):].mean() - m[:len(a)].mean() >= observed:
            count += 1
    return observed, count / n

blocks.html: One choice to make up front: one-sided ("is new better?") or two-sided ("is new different, either way?"). The simulation above counts shuffled gaps of 2.875 or more in either direction, so its p-value comes out about twice your one-sided one. Decide which question you're asking before you look at the data; switching afterwards to get a smaller p is a quiet form of cheating.

sections.title: What a p-value is not

blocks.html:
A p-value answers a narrow question. It's easy to stretch it into one it doesn't answer:

  • It is not the chance that H₀ is true. (That needs Bayes, chapter 11.)
  • It is not the size of the effect. A tiny, useless effect can have p = 0.0001 with enough data.
  • A big p-value does not prove "no effect". It may just mean too little data.

The 0.05 line is a convention, not a law of nature. Report the p-value and the effect size (with an interval, chapter 8).

blocks.q: An app tested a new button on 2 million users. Click rate went from 10.00% to 10.02%, with p = 0.003. Should they celebrate?

opts.t: Yes: p < 0.05 means the effect is large
Not much: the effect is real but tiny; whether 0.02 points matters is a business question, not a p-value question
No: p = 0.003 means the result is probably a fluke
No: a p-value can't be computed with 2 million users

blocks.why: With huge samples, even microscopic effects become "significant". Significance says the effect probably isn't zero; it says nothing about whether it's big enough to care about.

sections.title: Two ways to be wrong, and power

blocks.html:
A test can fail in two directions:

Really no effectReally an effect
Test says "effect!"False positive (type I)correct
Test says "nothing"correctFalse negative (type II)

The 0.05 threshold (called α) caps false positives at 5% when there's no effect. Power is the chance of catching an effect that is really there. It grows with the effect size and the sample size, and it's the reason you should decide the sample size before running an experiment.

blocks.code:
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
false_pos = 0
for trial in range(2000):
    a = rng.normal(0, 1, 30)
    b = rng.normal(0, 1, 30)
    se = np.sqrt(a.var(ddof=1) / 30 + b.var(ddof=1) / 30)
    if (b.mean() - a.mean()) / se > 1.645:
        false_pos += 1
print(false_pos / 2000)

sections.title: Twenty tests on pure noise

blocks.html:
Here's how good scientists fool themselves. Test 20 things (20 button colours, 20 subgroups, 20 outcome measures) where nothing is going on. Each test has a 5% false-positive rate, so the chance that at least one looks "significant" is 1 − 0.95²⁰ ≈ 64%. Report only that one and you've published noise. That's p-hacking.

The simplest fix, Bonferroni, uses α/20 for each of 20 tests, which keeps the chance of any false positive near 5%.

def p_value(a, b, n=5000, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    a, b = np.asarray(a, float), np.asarray(b, float)
    obs = b.mean() - a.mean()
    pooled = np.concatenate([a, b])
    hits = 0
    for _ in range(n):
        m = rng.permutation(pooled)
        hits += m[len(a):].mean() - m[:len(a)].mean() >= obs
    return hits / n

blocks.q: Explain a p-value to a friend who runs a bakery and tried a new recipe on some days, without using the words "null hypothesis".
blocks.a: Suppose the recipe made no difference at all. Then which days happened to get the new recipe is just luck of the draw. If I reshuffle which days count as "new recipe" thousands of times, I see how big a difference luck alone tends to make. The p-value is how often luck matched or beat the difference you actually saw. A small p-value means luck rarely does that, so the recipe probably did something. It doesn't say how much, or guarantee it, and if you try twenty recipes some will look good by luck.
